paper_title: Equal CER, Unequal Damage: Severity-Weighted Character Error Rate for OCR

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a typo as much as a wrong name. We introduce semCER, which keeps CER's alignment and denominator and charges each grapheme edit a severity from an LLM judge, with no word segmentation. Normalized CER keeps the score of a whole transcription, where it tracks readers as well as semCER or better, and semCER breaks that score down into named edits. The charges track readers' ratings edit by edit in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese and put the edits readers rate most severe near the top of a sorted list. On pairs drawn where CER and semCER disagreed, readers side with semCER more often than with normalized CER in English and Chinese, and equally often in Vietnamese. Across 16 languages, the judge charges a wrong diacritic or tone mark almost nothing in Spanish but nearly a wrong letter's severity in Telugu. Where we can count real words, a general VLM's wrong letter forms one far above chance while a classical pipeline's stays near it. We release the 61 million judged edits, the aggregated reader ratings, and the distilled scorer at https://github.com/nguyenx2t/semcer.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Consider two optical character recognition (OCR) systems that each make one error on an English line  (Fig. 1)  . One writes strategically as strategicallv, and the other misreads the agency acronym AGFD as ACFD. reader fixes the first without hesitation but cannot fix the second, which silently renames an organization. Yet Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and visionlanguage models (VLMs) alike (Ouyang et al., 2025; 1 Neudecker et al., 2021; Beyene and Dancy, 2026), charges the two the same, because it counts edits and divides by the reference length, whatever each edit costs the reader. Benchmarks and scoring toolkits soften the uniform charge by removing or folding whitespace, case, and punctuation before counting (Ouyang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Vaessen, 2025), but normalization still charges every surviving edit alike. In Fig. 1, two á. Readers rate the first recoverable from Vietnamese lines contain the same substitution, ấ its sentence and the second unrecoverable because it changes the heroines name, while normalization charges both the same. VLMs add failure mode of their own, since they decode through strong language prior and write fluent wrong words (Gardella et al., 2026; Karamolegkou et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026; Lee et al., 2026) that CER charges no more than typo. Metrics that do weigh meaning either rate the whole output, as semantic similarity scores and most LLM judges do, or grade spans marked outside CERs alignment, as MQM does (Freitag et al., 2021). Neither stays on CERs scale. rate that keeps CERs form and changes its charge raises three questions. (Q1) Which unit do we charge when script puts no spaces between words? (Q2) Are few severity classes fine enough to choose between two transcriptions that both read almost right? (Q3) Where does severity still help once benchmark has normalized cosmetic edits away? In this paper, we introduce semCER, which answers Q1 by design. It charges the grapheme clusters that CERs alignment already produces and keeps CERs denominator. One definition therefore applies to alphabets, abugidas, abjads, and unspaced scripts without word segmentation, and charging every edit one gives back CER exactly. For Q2, judge rates each edit on five-level rubric, and semCER reads the charge from the judges probabilities rather than its most likely level, so two edits at the same level can still differ. Whether that finer charge agrees with readers and chooses between two almost-right transcriptions better than three-class charge does (Q2), and whether it adds to normalization (Q3), are empirical questions. We answer them by testing semCER against readers, three-class charge, and normalized CER. The answers make semCER tool for finding and grading errors, while normalized CER remains the score for whole transcription. We make four contributions. semCER orders the errors to check. Sorted by charge, the edits readers rate most severe come near the top, an order CER cannot give. The charge tracks readers ratings beyond what the edits type predicts, and in English and Chinese beyond whether normalization would remove the edit (Section 5). Readers mostly side with semCER where it disagrees with CER. On pairs drawn where CER and semCER ranked two transcriptions in opposite order, readers of English and Chinese side with semCER on 71 and 78% of pairs. They side with normalized CER, the stronger baseline, on 58 and 60%, and Vietnamese readers side with the two equally often. On the same pairs, readers of all three languages side with semCER significantly more often than with three-class charge (Section 6). An equal edit count hides unequal damage, set by the language and by the system. The judges charge for an edit varies across 16 languages with the price of the smallest edit, which costs almost nothing in Spanish and nearly wrong letters severity in Telugu. Where general VLM and EasyOCR tie on edit count, the VLMs edits cost more in Chinese and Vietnamese and less in English, French, and Spanish. The split follows the price of the smallest edit, and at least three of the four VLMs show it in each language. The VLMs letter errors cost more than classical pipelines in every language where we can measure both, except Spanish, and they form real words where the pipelines form non-words, so word-list check misses them (Section 7). distilled scorer with fixed weights reproduces the judge. 0.8B student trained on the judges distributions, with no human rating, comes within 0.03 of the judges agreement with readers and orders nine in ten clear edit pairs as the judge does (Section 8). We release it with the 61 million judged edits and the aggregated per-item reader ratings.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Downstream harm. OCR errors matter unequally downstream. They corrupt entities and numbers in retrieval and question answering (van Strien et al., 2020; Hamdi et al., 2023; Jaud et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025), and low CER can hide decision-critical errors (He et al., 2025a). Error rates with graded charge. Speech recognition has several error rates that keep the word error rates form and replace its unit charge. EmbER discounts substitutions with similar word embeddings (Bañeras Roux et al., 2022), Semantic-WER weights entities and sentiment words (Roy, 2021), and SWWER weights words by BERT-derived importance (Zhang and Ai, 2024). Three others grade each error by its effect, minED (Bañeras-Roux et al., 2024), clinicians impact labels (Ellis et al., 2026), and the NER accuracy rate for live subtitling (Romero-Fresco and Martínez Pérez, 2015). Embedding similarity as semantic severity. BERTScore, BLEURT, SemDist, and H_eval compare the whole reference and hypothesis through embeddings or learned scores (Zhang et al., 2020; Sellam et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2021; Sasindran et al., 2023), and aligned variants score token or segment pairs (Rugayan et al., 2022; Sasindran et al., 2024). They charge similarity on scale unrelated to CERs, and BERTScore responds weakly to small errors in lexically close candidates, including changed figure (Hanna and Bojar, 2021; Huang et al., 2025), which are the errors OCR makes. Model-judged severity on spans. MQM annotates error spans by type and weights them by severity (Lommel et al., 2014; Freitag et al., 2021), and GEMBA-MQM, AutoMQM, xCOMET, and TIGERScore have model mark and grade the spans (Kocmi and Federmann, 2023; Fernandes et al., 2023; Guerreiro et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024). In grammatical error correction, CLEME2.0 also weights individual edits with language model (Ye et al., 2025). It aligns the erroneous source, the systems correction, and the reference corrections into word chunks and scores each chunk as hit, wrong, missing, or an unnecessary correction. It then weights chunk by embedding similarity or by an LLMs rating of how important the correction is and combines the four scores with fitted coefficients. JELV and LLM judges likewise rate correction from its marked edits (Zhan et al., 2026; Kobayashi et al., 2024). semCER has only reference and no erroneous source text, so it scores the recoverability of each error in the transcription, where CLEME2.0 scores the importance of each correction. It charges the graphemes of fixed unit-cost alignment, which needs no word segmentation, and keeps CERs denominator, so charging every edit one gives CER back. LLM judges for document transcription. LLM judges rate extracted tables (Horn and Keuper, 2026), penalize handwritten-math transcriptions that silently correct the writer (Seong et al., 2026), and sort the errors of text diff into minor and major (Gutteridge et al., 2026). Each scores whole output or counts errors by class. Normalization and cost tables. OCR benchmarks transform text differently before scoring (Ouyang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Rice and Nartker, 1996), and in speech the choice is known to distort evaluation, since Whispers normalizer strips Indic vowel signs and flatters the model (Manohar and Pillai, 2024; Thennal et al., 2025). second line of work replaces the uniform Levenshtein costs (Levenshtein, 1966) with learned or tuned ones, either weight per operation or character pair that is fitted once and reused (Ristad and Yianilos, 1998; Oncina and Sebban, 2006; Stanchev et al., 2019) or operation probabilities from learned encodings of both strings (Libovický and Fraser, 2022). Normalization rewrites the strings before alignment, and cost tables let the costs choose the alignment. semCER instead fixes unit-cost alignment first and charges its edits afterward. 3 Output-level OCR metrics. Other OCR metrics decompose page-level error by pipeline stage (Bourne et al., 2026), ignore reading order (Clausner et al., 2020), or score reconstruction fidelity against the page image (Vandepitte, 2026). SCORE, for generative parsing, adjusts the edit distance for representational variation and counts hallucinated and omitted tokens (Li et al., 2025). It normalizes the variation away before counting, while semCER charges what survives. Unit-test benchmarks replace the edit count with binary checks per page (Poznanski et al., 2025).

sections.title: 3 The semCER Metric
sections.content: semCER has two parts, definition that puts severity in place of CERs unit charge and judge that supplies the severity.

sections.title: 3.1 Definition
sections.content: semCER replaces each edits unit charge in CER with severity, so the first choice is what counts as one edit. Like CER, it charges characters rather than words, because script with no spaces between words yields word error rate only after segmentation step whose mistakes the score inherits (Thennal et al., 2025) (Q1). We treat character in both scores as an extended grapheme cluster, following Unicode Standard Annex #29 (Unicode Consortium, 2026) under Normalization Form C, so base letter with its accents or tone marks is one unit, as grapheme-level OCR metrics recommend (Nisfer et al., 2026). Published CER implementations often count code points instead (Vaessen, 2025), which splits syllable of an abugida into its consonant and vowel signs and counts an accented letter as one unit or several depending on how the text was encoded. Extended grapheme clusters approximate the characters reader perceives and give the same units whatever the encoding form, so the judge rates one kind of unit in every language. We compute every CER in this work over the same grapheme clusters, caseand whitespace-sensitive, and call it unnormalized CER. Let the reference and output be grapheme sequences = (r1, . . . , rm) and = (h1, . . . , hn). An optimal Levenshtein alignment (Levenshtein, 1966; Wagner and Fischer, 1974) yields (r, h) = (e1, . . . , eq) of substitutions, deletions, and insertions. We break the edit sequence ties among minimal alignments toward substitutions, then deletions, so the judge sees misread glyph as one edit, and CER is unchanged. For > 0, CER charges each edit one and divides by the reference length, CER(r, h) = 1 i=1 1 = . (1) semCER keeps this form and replaces the unit charge by severity si = s(ei; r, h) the judged cost of edit ei read in its line, [0, 1], semCER(r, h) = 1 i=1 si, (2) where zero marks surface change, low value recoverable edit, and one an unrecoverable loss of content. semCER therefore discounts the edits the judge rates recoverable. With every si = 1 it is CER itself, and it never exceeds CER, since no severity exceeds one. Figure 2 scores one line. The outputs lowercase follows the scan where the reference capitalizes it, so it costs nothing, and so does an added space. One wrong word, which the alignment splits into three edits, carries most of the charge, and dropped space the rest.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Corpus. We run the judge on the outputs of seven systems on 25 public datasets in 16 languages, 61 million edits in all, scored line by line after the filtering in Appendix A.2. The systems are of three kinds, two classical pipelines, document-specialized VLM, and four general VLMs  (Table 4)  . Human annotation. Native or fluent readers of English, Vietnamese, and Chinese annotated three pools, sized in Table 5 (Appendix A.3). The single-edit pool holds about 85 edits 5 Figure 3: Sorted by severity, the edits readers rate most severe come first. Each panel gives the share of all reader-rated damage caught after checking fraction of the single-edit pool in each order, over the first half of the list. The readers own order is the ceiling, random order the diagonal, and the rule marks the 10% cut. per language, each the only edit in its line, and tests whether the judge charges an edit as reader would. We drew it evenly from three bands of the judges severity, low, intermediate, and high, so the pool spans the scale. The pair-level pool, named for its reference and transcription pairs, holds about 180 whole transcriptions per language and tests the summed score. Readers rate both on the rubrics five levels. The preference pool holds about 175 pairs of transcriptions of one line per language, drawn where CER and semCER, on the judges earlier severities, ranked them in opposite order, and readers choose the better OCR of the reference. Baselines. We compare the severity with three charges that use no judge, table built from the judges corpus, and two coarser readouts of the same judge. The judge-free charges are CERs own per-edit charge, the filter label, and the real-word label. The filter label records whether an edit survives the character filter that OCR benchmarks apply before scoring, which keeps letters and digits and drops whitespace, punctuation, and symbols (Ouyang et al., 2025), and the real-word label whether the edit forms real word. The type table charges an edit the corpus-mean severity of its type and reads the judges corpus but not the line. The coarser readouts are the class charge, the judges most likely level charged on three fixed class weights, and the whole-line judgment, one rating of the whole line. Normalized CER applies the filter and folds case before alignment. Statistics. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from 10,000 draws, resampling items within band for the single-edit partial correlations and source documents elsewhere. The single-edit partial correlations control for the sampling band, since we drew that pool by the judges severity. partial whose interval excludes zero therefore shows agreement within band, which the draw alone cannot produce. We take comparisons p-value as twice the smaller bootstrap tail probability about zero and call difference significant at α = 0.05 after Holm correction (Holm, 1979) within the families that Appendix A.4 names.

On the single-edit pool each edit sits in its own line, so an order of the pool runs across lines. The top-of-list share summarizes that curve over cuts at 10 to 50% of the list, scaled so that random order scores 0 and the readers own order 1 (Appendix B.1). For strategicallv in Fig. 1, it charges 0.59, the mean for swap. The judge, which reads the line, charges 0.25, and readers give 0.20. sections.title: 6 Reader Preferences Where CER and semCER Disagree
sections.content: On whole transcriptions, normalized CER tracks readers as well as semCER or better. Its Spearmans ρ is 0.93, 0.90, and 0.76 against semCERs 0.89, 0.87, and 0.76  (Table 7)  . semCERs value beside CER therefore lies where the two scores rank pair of transcriptions of one line in opposite order. We ask how often readers side with semCER there, and whether it adds to what normalization already catches. Where the scores disagree. We drew the preference pool from such disagreements on the judges earlier severities, one pair per source line, and readers chose the better transcription in each. score agrees with pair when it picks the output strict majority of readers chose, tie counting as miss. When the pool was drawn, unnormalized CER picked the other output on every pair, so its agreement was one minus semCERs, and the baseline is therefore normalized CER, which can side with either. On the whole pool, readers of English and Chinese side with semCER on more than seven pairs in ten, against about six in ten for normalized CER. Vietnamese readers side with the two scores equally often, at about eight in ten (Table 2, top). Near-miss pairs. Two nested subsets sharpen the test. In near-miss pair, the output that CER rates worse is mostly right and has an error that normalization would keep (Appendix C.2). Before the test, we fixed the criterion that semCER lead normalized CER significantly in at least two languages on these pairs. It does, in English and Chinese  (Table 8)  . sections.title: 8 A Distilled Scorer with Fixed Weights
sections.content: A small model with fixed weights approximates the judge, so anyone can compute semCER locally. Scoring edits through an API costs money at scale and ties the scores to whichever model the provider serves. We distill the judge into student, Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base (Qwen Team, 2026a), which we fine-tune to read the pair with the edit marked and predict the judges distribution over the rubric levels, read out as in Eq. (4). We hold out every ratedpool line under every system and use no human rating for training or model selection (Appendix E). The student ships as Python package, installed with pip install semcer. The student nearly matches the judges agreement with readers. It correlates with their ratings at 0.79, 0.63, and 0.80 in English, Vietnamese, and Chinese, against the judges 0.81, 0.66, and 0.82. On pairs of edits whose judge severities differ by at least half rubric step, it orders nine in ten as the judge does, and its severity differs from the judges by mean absolute 0.04 per edit (Appendix E).

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: CER counts edits, and normalization decides which edits to count, but neither says what an edit costs the reader. We introduced semCER, which charges each grapheme edit judged severity, without word segmentation, and keeps CERs alignment and denominator. The two scores divide the work. Normalized CER tracks readers ratings of whole transcriptions as well as semCER or better, so it remains the score for transcription. An equal edit count is tie for CER, and semCER breaks it with charges that follow the languages smallest edit and the systems kind of error. Where the two scores order pair of transcriptions the other way, readers of English and Chinese mostly side with semCER. They do so most of all where normalization leaves CERs choice in place, and readers of all three languages side with semCER over three-class charge. The score is sum over the aligned edits, so each decision between two transcriptions breaks down into named edits and their charges. Those charges track readers ratings edit by edit in three languages and put the errors readers rate most severe near the top of sorted list. We therefore recommend normalized CER for scoring transcription. Beside it, semCER, computed locally with the distilled scorer, chooses between transcriptions where CER ties or the two scores disagree, and names the edits behind the choice.

sections.title: 10 Limitations
sections.content: Languages. Readers validated the severity in three languages. In the other thirteen, the grapheme load comes from the judge alone, and the judges severities may shift with languages resource level (Joshi et al., 2020). The lowest-resource languages in our corpus all use non-Latin scripts, so we cannot separate resource level from script. We have not tested whether graphemes are the right unit in Thai, which writes no word boundaries, or in the abjads, which leave vowels unwritten. Construct. Readers rated on the rubrics levels, and preference readers chose after guidelines that teach the same construct. The human studies therefore test whether the judge applies the rubric as readers do and leave open whether recoverability is the right construct. The rubrics levels depend on whether an output is valid word, so part of the higher charge 10 the judge places on general VLM letter errors in Section 7, which more often form real words, comes from the rubric itself. We leave semCERs value for downstream tasks to future work. Judge version. The provider replaced the judges checkpoint during this work, so severity is comparable only within one checkpoint. Corpus severities come from the checkpoint before the replacement. In the rated pools only the edits the judge first left undecided were re-judged on the one after, and the English and Chinese margins on the preference pool and its normalization-proof pairs hold under both (Appendix C.3). The local student has fixed weights, so it avoids this boundary at the cost of approximating the judge. Rating. Readers rated each single edit as the only edit in its line and rated whole transcriptions without marked edits, so no reader rated an edits severity inside line with other damage. The judge charges each grapheme edit separately, so wrong word that the alignment splits into several edits pays once per edit  (Fig. 2)  . Risks. low semCER says that reader could recover the errors, and transcription with low score still needs checking before use. judge that undercharges an error class would hide that class.

sections.title: Use of AI Assistants
sections.content: Large language models are part of the method. They judge each edits severity, second one re-judges every rated transcription, and the distilled scorer is fine-tuned language model. For this manuscript, we used the same class of tools for copy editing (grammar, clarity, and formatting) and for drafting support. We also used language models and agents for literature search, code writing, debugging, and informal discussion and brainstorming. The authors are solely responsible for the scientific content, study design, experiments, and conclusions.

sections.content: DeepSeek-V4-Flash Preview scores each marked edit at temperature 1, answering directly without reasoning trace. It sees the full reference and output, then the edit in brackets, and returns one of the five rubric levels of Table 1. Prompt. The system message is the text below, the same for every per-edit severity in this paper, while the whole-line judgment of Appendix B.2 uses its own prompt. The user message gives the reference and output in full as REFERENCE: and HYPOTHESIS: blocks, then the edit block in the system messages notation with ten graphemes of context on each side and an ellipsis beyond, then the line Output exactly one digit (0, 1, 2, 3, or 4):. You are an OCR quality evaluator. For each request, rate how much single grapheme-level edit damages semantic meaning, given the surrounding context. TASK: You are given an edit operation and two views of the same sentence REF with the edit position marked in brackets, and HYP with the edit position marked in brackets. Score the damage on integer scale 0-4 based on the rubric. 1. Read REF and HYP to establish sentence-level context. 2. Identify the operation type and locate the edit at the bracket position. 3. Determine if the hypothesis token is valid word/morpheme in the language. 4. Determine if the sentence-level context signals an error and if the original is recoverable. 5. Apply SEVERITY LEVELS strictly. Do not score on intuition. 6. Output exactly one digit: 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4. No reasoning text. LANGUAGES: Any natural language. Apply identical criteria regardless of script. EDIT NOTATION: - SUB: REF contains [X], HYP contains [Y] - DEL: REF contains [X], HYP contains [] - INS: REF contains [], HYP contains [Y] SEVERITY LEVELS: 0 Surface only. Case, punctuation, whitespace, or glyph variant. Meaning fully preserved; change would not be noticed in normal reading. 1 Minor. Hypothesis is non-word but sentence-level context uniquely determines the original. Reader recovers with negligible effort. 2 Moderate. Hypothesis is valid word but contextually plausible-but-odd in local syntax. Reader may parse at face value or sense an error; recovery requires noticing the mismatch. 3 Severe with partial recovery. Result signals an error (grammatical anomaly, format violation, collocational mismatch) but the original cannot be uniquely recovered from candidate set. 4 Total. Hypothesis is fully valid, fits surrounding context, gives no signal of error, original unrecoverable from this edit alone. Magnitude doesn't matter; what matters is recoverability. ANCHOR (Score 4): Operation: SUB REF: The team meeting will be held at [3]pm tomorrow in the conference room. HYP: The team meeting will be held at [8]pm tomorrow in the conference room. Why 4: Sentence context "team meeting ... conference room" doesn't disambiguate the time. "8pm" is fully valid. Reader has no path to recover "3pm". Information destroyed. EXAMPLES: Operation: SUB REF: will meet you at 3p[m] tomorrow at the cafe. HYP: will meet you at 3p[M] tomorrow at the cafe. Score: 0 Operation: SUB REF: The patient is im[p]roving rapidly after surgery. HYP: The patient is im[b]roving rapidly after surgery. Score: 1 Operation: SUB REF: Please turn l[e]ft at the next corner near the bank. HYP: Please turn l[i]ft at the next corner near the bank. Score: 17 Operation: SUB REF: She lives on the [1]3th floor of the building. HYP: She lives on the [2]3th floor of the building. Score: 3 Operation: SUB REF: She was born in 19[9]9 in small village. HYP: She was born in 19[8]9 in small village. Score: 4 OUTPUT FORMAT: Exactly one digit: 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4. Nothing else. Undecided edits. When the judge returns no digit or puts less than half of its probability on the five digits, we ask it once more. If it fails again, we charge the edit one, the highest severity, the conservative choice for an edit the judge cannot decide. This imputed charge affects 0.8% of corpus edits, between 1.6 and 4.3% in the three rated languages and under 0.01% elsewhere. It enters only the corpus-level semCER scores. The analyses of Section 7 use only transcriptions the judge scored completely, and we re-judged every undecided edit in the rated pools, so no rated edit carries an imputed charge (Appendix C.3). A.2 Corpus, systems, and compute Corpus. We drop non-transcription tasks, references shorter than 20 or longer than 4,000 code points, records with only numbers or bare URLs, and formula-dense text. reference counts as formula-dense when it is under 200 code points with three or more LATEX commands, or under 100 with more than fifth of its characters mathematical symbols. We then keep at most 15,000 lines per dataset and language for handwriting and printed documents and 3,000 lines per language for scene text, pooled across datasets  (Table 3)  . Systems. Qianfan-OCR and the general VLMs  (Table 4)  receive the prompt Read all the text visible in this image. Output only the text, nothing else. EasyOCR, PP-OCRv5, and Qianfan-OCR ran on one RTX 3090, and the four general VLMs took about 40 H100-hours in all under vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Judging the corpus cost about $2,000, and the distilled scorer trained for about 30 hours on one A100. Release. We use each dataset for research under its terms. We release severities and ratings under CC BY 4.0, with source text only where its license permits redistribution, and the scorers code and weights under Apache-2.0. The other sources carry labels only, keyed by line identifier to match the original datasets. A.3 Human studies Readers. Readers were native or fluent speakers naive to the research, recruited through Prolific and by invitation and paid $12 per hour, the platforms recommended rate. They saw no system names, judge output, or study hypothesis, and no author rated items. Table 5 gives their agreement. Consent. Readers recruited through Prolific saw study description naming the purpose (evaluating how well OCR systems preserve meaning), the task, and its length. All readers could stop at any time and consented by starting. No ethics board reviewed the study. Data. Readers judged transcriptions of public documents, and we asked nothing about them. We stored only pseudonymous rater IDs, ratings, optional rationales, and response times. Since the description did not mention publishing ratings, we release per-item aggregates, the mean rating or majority choice and the number of readers, and no individual responses, IDs, or rationales.
